items.prompt: A service needs to alert when customer error rate exceeds its SLO, not merely when CPU is high. Which design is best?
constraints: CPU can be normal during dependency failure.

options.text: Publish a customer-facing error metric, alarm on the defined SLO threshold and window, and link the alarm to an actionable runbook.
Alarm only when every instance exceeds 90% CPU.
Use log retention as the availability signal.
Create a dashboard without an alarm or owner.

feedback.Reason: A customer outcome metric detects availability loss that infrastructure saturation may not reveal.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudWatch metrics and alarms evaluate a time series against a threshold or anomaly and can trigger operational actions.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team counts valid failures, chooses an SLO-aligned window, and routes the alarm to a recovery owner.
Details.errorCorrection: CPU is indirect, retention is storage policy, and a dashboard without action does not provide detection.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Metric definitions and dimensions need consistency to avoid noisy or misleading alerts.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: CPU does not prove customer success or failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Log retention does not measure availability.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A dashboard alone does not notify or assign response.

items.prompt: An API is slow, but application CPU and memory are normal. Which tool best helps find the slow downstream call?

options.text: Use AWS X-Ray distributed traces with propagated context and inspect segment and subsegment timing for the request path.
Increase API timeout until users stop seeing errors.
Use only an aggregate instance CPU graph.
Disable tracing because it cannot show dependency timing.

feedback.Reason: Distributed tracing links one request across services and exposes where time is spent.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: X-Ray segments and subsegments record service and downstream timing when trace context is propagated.
Details.scenarioApplication: Operators inspect the slow path, correlate it with logs and metrics, and fix the dependency or apply a bounded mitigation.
Details.errorCorrection: Longer timeouts hide latency, CPU is indirect, and tracing is specifically intended to show distributed request paths.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Tracing has sampling and cost considerations and should avoid sensitive data in annotations.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A longer timeout delays failure and does not remove the slow dependency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Aggregate CPU cannot locate cross-service latency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Dependency timing is a primary use of distributed tracing.

items.prompt: An application writes structured errors to CloudWatch Logs, but no metric exists for failed payments. What should be added?
constraints: The log event contains a stable error field.
The metric must avoid counting unrelated text.

options.text: Create a precise metric filter or application metric for the payment error, validate its dimensions, and alarm on an actionable rate.
Alarm on any log line containing the word error.
Delete the logs after ingestion to avoid duplicate alerts.
Use disk space as a proxy for payment success.

feedback.Reason: A precise metric derived from structured events turns an important application failure into an observable signal.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudWatch metric filters or embedded metrics can count selected log events and feed alarms and dashboards.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner filters a stable field, controls dimensions, tests positive and negative cases, and routes the alarm to payment operations.
Details.errorCorrection: Broad text filters create noise, early deletion harms diagnosis, and disk space is unrelated to payment correctness.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Metric filters and high-cardinality dimensions can cost money and should be designed for action.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Generic error text can include unrelated or expected failures.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Deleting logs removes evidence and does not solve metric design.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Disk space does not measure payment outcomes.

items.prompt: A service should page only when customer errors are high and a dependency is unavailable, while lower-level signals remain visible. Which CloudWatch design fits?
constraints: Individual alarms remain useful for diagnosis.

options.text: Use individual metric alarms plus a composite alarm for the paging condition, with a runbook that preserves the underlying signals.
Delete the dependency alarm and page only on CPU.
Combine all metrics into one unexplainable average.
Suppress all alarms until the monthly review.

feedback.Reason: Composite alarms combine conditions for notification without discarding the component evidence needed for diagnosis.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudWatch composite alarms use alarm states as inputs and can reduce notification noise while retaining metric alarms.
Details.scenarioApplication: Operators page on the correlated customer-impact condition and inspect the dependency and error alarms in the runbook.
Details.errorCorrection: CPU is indirect, opaque averages lose causal detail, and delayed review does not protect live availability.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Poorly chosen correlations can delay detection or suppress distinct failures, so each input needs an owner.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Removing dependency evidence can miss the actual cause.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Averages hide which condition caused the incident.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Monthly review is too slow for live failure response.

items.prompt: A load balancer health endpoint returns success even when the application cannot reach its required database. How should health be designed?
constraints: A deep check can remove all targets if the database fails.

options.text: Choose health-check depth deliberately: use a safe dependency-aware readiness signal for routing where appropriate, and separately monitor end-to-end customer success and dependency failures.
Make the health endpoint run a destructive write on every check.
Use only host CPU as the health check.
Remove health checks and route to every target.

feedback.Reason: Health checks should protect routing without creating a fragile or destructive dependency test, while business impact remains separately observable.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Readiness and liveness have different purposes; routing checks should be safe and aligned with whether a target can serve the intended request.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team defines a lightweight safe readiness path and uses request SLIs and dependency alarms for deeper behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: Destructive checks harm data, CPU does not show readiness, and routing to unhealthy targets worsens impact.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Deep dependency checks can prevent bad traffic but can also eject every target during a shared dependency failure.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A health check must not perform destructive business operations.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: CPU does not establish application or dependency readiness.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Removing checks sends traffic to known unhealthy targets.

items.prompt: A high-volume API needs traces for rare errors but cannot trace every successful request at full cost. Which choice is appropriate?
constraints: The trace must preserve enough context for diagnosis.

options.text: Use a deliberate sampling strategy that retains error or high-latency traces and samples normal traffic, then validate diagnostic coverage.
Disable tracing because sampling can never be useful.
Trace only successful requests to reduce storage.
Capture every request indefinitely without cost review.

feedback.Reason: Sampling can control observability cost while preserving traces that explain important failures.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: X-Ray sampling rules determine which requests are recorded; error and latency-focused capture improves signal per trace.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team tests rules against rare errors, preserves correlation identifiers, and reviews coverage and cost.
Details.errorCorrection: Disabling tracing loses distributed evidence, successful-only data misses failures, and unlimited capture has cost and privacy risks.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Sampling can miss a new failure class, so rules and metrics should be reviewed after incidents.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Sampling is a way to control cost rather than a reason to remove traces.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Successful traces do not explain rare failures.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Unlimited retention and capture is not an operationally bounded design.

items.prompt: A team adds a unique customer ID as a CloudWatch metric dimension for every request. What risk should it review?

options.text: Avoid uncontrolled high cardinality; use bounded actionable dimensions and put detailed identifiers in logs or traces with appropriate access controls.
Add more unique dimensions because more detail always improves alarms.
Disable all dimensions so regional failures are invisible.
Use customer IDs as alarm names instead of metrics.

feedback.Reason: Unbounded metric dimensions increase cost and make aggregation and alerting difficult; detailed context belongs in suitable telemetry.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudWatch metric dimensions create distinct time series, so cardinality should be bounded and tied to an operational question.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team keeps Region, service, route, and status dimensions where actionable and uses structured logs or traces for individual requests.
Details.errorCorrection: More dimensions can overwhelm cost and dashboards, no dimensions hide failure scope, and alarm names are not a metric model.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Detailed logs and traces also need retention and privacy governance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: High cardinality can make metrics expensive and hard to operate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Removing all dimensions loses useful failure-domain context.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Alarm names cannot replace time-series measurement.

items.prompt: Recovery evidence must remain available for 90 days, but application logs currently expire after seven days. What should change?
constraints: Logs are needed for incident review.

options.text: Set an appropriate CloudWatch Logs retention policy or export to governed storage, protect access, and verify the retained evidence is searchable or recoverable.
Keep seven days because logs are not part of recovery evidence.
Make all logs public so auditors can access them.
Disable log collection during incidents to reduce cost.

feedback.Reason: Retention is part of operational evidence and must match the recovery and audit requirement.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudWatch Logs retention or export controls determine how long evidence remains available and who can access it.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner configures retention, encryption and permissions, and tests retrieval during an incident review exercise.
Details.errorCorrection: Short retention loses evidence, public logs violate confidentiality, and disabling collection during incidents removes the most useful data.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Longer retention costs storage and requires lifecycle and sensitive-data controls.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Logs can be necessary to reconstruct and learn from recovery.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Audit access must not expose sensitive logs publicly.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Incident-time suppression creates an observability blind spot.

items.prompt: A metric stops arriving when an exporter fails, but the alarm treats missing data as not breaching. What should the team review?
constraints: Missing data can indicate telemetry failure.

options.text: Choose missing-data treatment deliberately, alarm on telemetry health separately, and test exporter failure so silence cannot hide service risk.
Always treat missing data as good because it reduces noise.
Delete the metric when the exporter fails.
Assume a missing metric means zero errors.

feedback.Reason: Telemetry absence can be a monitoring failure and should not silently look like a healthy service.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudWatch alarms have explicit missing-data behavior, and telemetry pipelines need their own health signals.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner chooses semantics for each metric, alerts on missing critical telemetry, and runs a failure test.
Details.errorCorrection: Treating silence as good can suppress incidents, deleting metrics removes evidence, and no data is not zero errors.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Some sparse metrics need neutral missing treatment, so the choice must reflect the metric's emission contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Silence can represent exporter or service failure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Missing data cannot be interpreted as successful requests without an emission contract.

items.prompt: An incident dashboard contains hundreds of raw instance metrics but no customer, dependency, or recovery signals. What should be added first?
constraints: Dependencies and recovery steps are known.

options.text: Organize a service-level view with customer SLIs, dependency health, saturation, regional scope, recovery progress, and links to detailed diagnostics and runbooks.
Add more raw CPU graphs from every instance.
Remove all detailed metrics so the dashboard is smaller.
Use a dashboard with no time range or alarm state.

feedback.Reason: An operational dashboard should support detection, diagnosis, and recovery decisions at the service level.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Layered observability joins user outcomes, dependencies, resources, deployment state, and recovery milestones.
Details.scenarioApplication: The primary view shows whether users are affected and what action is safe, with drill-down links for technical analysis.
Details.errorCorrection: More raw graphs add noise, deleting detail harms diagnosis, and missing time or alarm context makes the view ambiguous.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A dashboard is not a substitute for alarms or runbooks; each panel should have a decision owner.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Raw resource volume does not answer service or recovery questions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Removing detail prevents investigation after detection.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A dashboard without context cannot support incident decisions.

items.prompt: Operators can see a slow X-Ray trace but cannot find the corresponding application logs. What correlation should be added?
constraints: The service emits traces and structured logs.

options.text: Propagate a request or trace correlation identifier into structured logs and traces, then link telemetry without placing credentials or sensitive payloads in it.
Use the instance ID as the only request identifier.
Log full authorization tokens so every trace can be found.
Disable logs and rely on traces alone.

feedback.Reason: A shared safe correlation identifier links distributed evidence without requiring sensitive payloads.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Trace IDs and structured log fields let operators pivot from a user request to service and dependency records.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team propagates context across asynchronous and synchronous boundaries and redacts sensitive fields.
Details.errorCorrection: Instance ID does not identify one request, tokens are secrets, and traces alone may omit application details.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Context propagation across queues and retries needs explicit semantics and can add telemetry volume.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: One instance handles many requests and cannot identify a specific trace.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Authorization tokens must not be placed in observability fields.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Logs often contain application details that traces do not.

items.prompt: A multi-Region service has a healthy global aggregate but one Region is failing. Which operational view is needed?

options.text: Show regional customer SLIs, dependency health, capacity, and routing state alongside the global aggregate, with regional alarms and ownership.
Show only the global average to reduce alarm count.
Use only the primary Region dashboard during recovery.
Remove Region dimensions from every metric.

feedback.Reason: A global aggregate can hide an isolated regional failure, so operators need failure-domain visibility.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Regional dimensions and dashboards expose scope, while the aggregate retains a service-wide view.
Details.scenarioApplication: Operators identify the affected Region, validate failover, and compare the survivor's capacity and user outcome.
Details.errorCorrection: Averages dilute failures, primary-only views omit the affected path, and removing dimensions loses diagnosis.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More regional signals require threshold and ownership discipline to avoid noise.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Global averages can hide regional customer impact.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The primary view is not enough when the primary is affected.

items.prompt: A recovery team needs to verify that an endpoint is usable after failover from outside the VPC. Which service is useful?
constraints: The test must run from a user-like location.
The journey is safe and repeatable.

options.text: Use a CloudWatch Synthetics canary with safe credentials and test data to exercise the endpoint, expected response, and latency from relevant locations.
Check only the private subnet route table.
Use EC2 instance count as the external user signal.
Run the check manually once a year.

feedback.Reason: A canary exercises the user-facing path and can run continuously after a recovery transition.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Synthetics runs scripted requests from configured canary locations and records success and latency.
Details.scenarioApplication: The canary validates DNS, authentication, application response, and cleanup without performing destructive actions.
Details.errorCorrection: Route tables are lower-level, instance count is indirect, and annual manual checks leave long blind periods.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Canaries cost money and need safe test data, credential rotation, and false-positive handling.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A route table does not prove the external journey.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Instance count does not measure endpoint behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Infrequent manual checks do not provide operational detection.

items.prompt: A recovery alarm fires but operators do not know whether to fail over, scale, or roll back. What is the missing operational property?

options.text: Link the alarm to a runbook with diagnosis, safe first actions, decision criteria, owners, rollback, and escalation paths.
Let the first operator choose any action without guardrails.
Suppress the alarm until a manager is available.
Replace the alarm with a dashboard link only.

feedback.Reason: An alarm is operationally useful when its context and response are explicit.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Runbooks translate signal into bounded diagnostic and mitigation steps and identify who owns the decision.
Details.scenarioApplication: The responder checks scope and dependency signals before executing a reversible action and records the result.
Details.errorCorrection: Unbounded choice can worsen the outage, suppression delays response, and dashboards do not define safe action.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Runbooks require maintenance after architecture changes and should include unavailable states rather than fake success.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Unbounded incident actions increase blast radius.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Waiting can extend the outage without reducing uncertainty.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A dashboard link lacks decision and rollback guidance.

items.prompt: A service is available but response latency rises as the connection pool approaches its limit. Which metric combination explains the risk?
constraints: The database CPU may remain normal.

options.text: Correlate user latency and error rate with pool utilization, connection wait time, request concurrency, and downstream latency.
Monitor only database storage capacity.
Use average CPU as the sole saturation signal.
Disable pool metrics because they expose internal details.

feedback.Reason: Saturation can occur at a connection boundary before a host or database reaches high CPU.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Queueing and pool utilization are leading indicators that explain tail latency and imminent overload.
Details.scenarioApplication: Operators compare the signals, cap concurrency, tune pooling, or load-shed before users experience a full outage.
Details.errorCorrection: Storage and CPU do not show connection wait, and hiding the bottleneck metric removes the useful signal.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More telemetry needs cost and retention control, but connection saturation is actionable.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Storage capacity does not explain connection queueing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: CPU is an indirect and potentially late signal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Internal saturation is necessary to protect external availability.

items.prompt: A service's infrastructure is green, but a customer cannot complete login because an external identity dependency is failing. Which signal should detect this?
constraints: The login journey is safe to test.
The dependency is outside the service fleet.

options.text: Use a synthetic login journey or equivalent customer SLI, alongside dependency and infrastructure metrics, to observe the external failure path.
Use only the application process health endpoint.
Use instance disk utilization.
Assume the identity provider's status page is the service SLI.

feedback.Reason: A customer journey can expose an external dependency failure that local infrastructure checks cannot see.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Synthetic checks and request SLIs measure the user path, while dependency metrics provide diagnosis and scope.
Details.scenarioApplication: The canary uses isolated credentials, validates expected authentication behavior, and alerts without exposing secrets.
Details.errorCorrection: Process health and disk utilization are local signals, and a provider status page is not the application's customer SLI.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Synthetic checks need safe credentials and can fail due to test setup, so they should be correlated with other evidence.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A local endpoint can remain healthy while authentication fails.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Disk utilization does not measure login success.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A provider status page is not a direct measure of this service's user journey.

items.prompt: A recovery exercise records no baseline from normal operation, so operators cannot tell whether the standby is healthy after cutover. What should be added?
constraints: Normal and recovery metrics are comparable.
The service has a defined success SLI.
The standby is monitored before traffic.

options.text: Define normal and recovery baselines for success, latency, saturation, replication lag, and dependency health, then compare them during the exercise.
Use only the recovery CPU value without a normal reference.
Stop collecting metrics in the primary before failover.
Declare the standby healthy if it accepts a TCP connection.

feedback.Reason: A recovery measurement needs a known reference and acceptance state to distinguish healthy degradation from failure.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Baselines turn raw metrics into comparable evidence for user outcome, latency, saturation, and replication behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team captures normal ranges, exercises failover, and checks whether recovery remains within the SLO and capacity assumptions.
Details.errorCorrection: CPU without context is indirect, stopping primary metrics removes comparison, and TCP does not prove application health.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Baselines vary with demand, so the exercise should include representative load and documented tolerance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A single value without baseline or SLI context is ambiguous.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Primary metrics are needed to compare the transition.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: TCP reachability does not prove the recovered user path.

items.prompt: After a regional outage, the team has logs, traces, and metrics but cannot reconstruct the timeline because clocks and identifiers differ. What improvement is most useful?
constraints: Incident review needs a common timeline.

options.text: Standardize timestamps, trace and request correlation, service and Region dimensions, retention, and a review dashboard that links to runbooks and raw evidence.
Collect more unstructured logs without a correlation model.
Delete old telemetry after every incident.
Use only one service's local clock and logs.

feedback.Reason: Consistent context makes distributed telemetry usable for incident reconstruction and recovery improvement.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Common time, correlation identifiers, dimensions, and retention allow operators to follow a request and failure across services and Regions.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner updates instrumentation standards, protects sensitive fields, and uses the evidence to fix recovery gaps.
Details.errorCorrection: More unstructured logs increase search cost, deletion removes learning evidence, and one local service view omits the distributed path.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Telemetry standards and retention require engineering and governance effort but reduce repeated incident ambiguity.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: More volume without structure does not create a timeline.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Deleting evidence prevents post-incident learning and audit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A distributed incident cannot be reconstructed from one local view.
